newsitem.title: USA: Critical week of talks on federal budget.
newsitem.headline: Critical week of talks on federal budget.

text.p: Budget negotiations between the White House and Congress entered a "make or break" week Monday as Republicans called for President Clinton to accept deeper reductions in Medicare spending.

Republicans have given the president five more days to work out an agreement to balance the budget by 2002 or they say they will negotiate a budget with conservatives in Clinton's own Democratic party.

Senate Budget Committee Chairman Pete Domenici, who welcomed the administration's offer last week to find more savings in the Medicare health programme, early in the day called on Clinton to offer up another $10 billion to $30 billion over the five years. This would slow the growth in the programme by $110 billion to $130 billion through 2002.

Domenici, a veteran of nearly two decades in the budget wars, said he is willing to give the closed-door talks until the end of the week before he starts to work on a final budget with fellow Republicans and conservative Democrats.
"This Friday will be make it or break it," he said in speech to the Associated General Contractors.

"The president moved slightly in our direction within these last five days of negotiations, but not enough yet," the New Mexico Republican said. "We are off somewhere between $10 billion and $30 billion in terms of where we ought to be."

The talks were being held in a basement room of the Capitol. White House budget director Frank Raines and congressional liason John Hilley are leading the president's budget team. Domenici, House Budget Committee Chairman John Kasich of Ohio and their Democratic counterparts, Sen. Frank Lautenberg of New Jersey and Representative John Spratt of South Carolina, have been representing Congress.

The budget is a blueprint for federal spending and taxes and does not go to the president for his signature into law but kicks off months of wrangling over details on programme changes and tax laws. Clinton will have a choice to sign or veto this separate legislation that implements spending cuts, changes in federal programmes and new tax laws.

Budget deficits declined in the four years of Clinton's first term and this year's deficit is expected to be $107 billion. But with growth in spending on health care and other mandatory spending all sides agree major changes are necessary to keep the deficit from ballooning in the next decade.
The two most politically sensitive issues, Medicare, which provides health care to nearly everyone over age 65, and possible cuts in taxes, are expected to be among the last issues resolved.

At first glance, the two objectives of bringing the deficit to zero and reducing taxes would seem mutually exclusive. But Republicans have argued that lower taxes on investment profits would boost the economy and that greater growth yields higher general tax revenue.
Clinton has proposed $98 billion in tax cuts over five years while Senate Republicans have suggested $177 billion. House Republicans have not set a target amount.
"Clearly, there will be a tax cut. And clearly that will be one of the items we will agree upon if we agree upon an overall budget," Domenici said.
Republicans are looking for tax relief for families with children, for those who inherit small businesses and farms, and for those with gains on investments.

On a brighter note, Domenici said negotiators had little differences remaining over the defence budget. Congressional sources said the two were about $3 billion apart with Republicans seeking the higher $268 billion level for 1998.
